Self-Harm Threats as Leverage.short_definition: Saying one will hurt or kill oneself if the other person leaves or refuses, which ties their decision to the speaker's survival.
Self-Harm Threats as Leverage.core_meaning: Saying one will hurt or kill oneself if the other person leaves or refuses, which ties their decision to the speaker's survival.
Self-Harm Threats as Leverage.expanded_definition: These are statements about suicide or self-injury that are tied to a particular choice the other person is making: leaving, ending a call, saying no. The same words can come from real despair, and from the outside the two can look identical, so every such statement deserves a serious response. The link to a demand is the tell: the statements arrive when a boundary does, and the person hearing them ends up responsible for another person's life.
Self-Harm Threats as Leverage.plain_language_summary: Someone says they will hurt themselves if you go or say no, and your choice suddenly feels like it carries their life. The fear and the crisis can both be real.
Self-Harm Threats as Leverage.why_this_matters: Hearing that your decision could cost a life is one of the heaviest things a person can carry. Many people stop making ordinary choices, like ending an evening or taking a trip, because the stakes feel too high, while the underlying distress goes unaddressed.
what_it_is: Statements about suicide or self-injury that arrive just as you move toward a separation, a refusal or a plan of your own.
A link drawn between your choice and the speaker's safety, so that one answer feels like the only safe one.
Sometimes said once on a terrible night, sometimes repeated each time a boundary is tried.
Often followed by a request for reassurance, a promise or a cancelled plan, and not by a step toward getting help.
Said face to face, in a late-night text or in a voicemail left after you have gone.
Hard to read from outside, because the same sentence can be a plea for rescue. That is why it is never brushed off.
what_it_sounds_like: If you walk out that door tonight, I don't know what I'll do to myself.
I'll end it. Then you'll be free of me.
You're the only reason I'm still here, so if you go, that's it.
Go ahead and sleep at your sister's. You'll find out in the morning.
I swear I'll do it this time.
I'm not safe right now, and it's because of you.
Answer me in five minutes or you'll have my death on your hands.
what_it_is_not: A person in real crisis who says they are thinking of suicide, with no link to anything you are doing. That calls for care, not analysis.
Telling a friend or counselor 'I've been having dark thoughts' in order to get help, with no demand attached.
A safety plan made with a therapist, where the person texts you a code word when they are struggling.
Flat exhaustion after a loss, such as 'I can't do this any more', that signals depletion and not a plan.
A statement of hopelessness made on a day when you were not leaving or refusing anything.
Someone overwhelmed at a breakup who blurts out the biggest words they have because they cannot find another way to say how bad it is.
this_may_be_it_when: The statement arrives within minutes of you saying you are leaving, declining or ending a conversation.
It names you as the cause, or as the only person who can prevent it.
Offers of a crisis line, a doctor or a relative are waved off in favor of your presence.
The same kind of statement has followed several separate disagreements, each time attached to something you wanted.
The talk of harm fades once you agree to stay or cancel, and returns at the next decision.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They bring it up on a calm day and ask for help finding a therapist or doctor.
They accept help from other people and are not asking you to be the only thing keeping them safe.
The statements have no link to any decision you made.
They tell you ahead of a hard anniversary or appointment so you can check in, without asking you to change your plans.
They already have treatment or a safety plan and are using it.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Despair can peak in the middle of a breakup, and people reach for the biggest words they have.
Someone who has had suicidal thoughts before may truly believe that a loss would be unsurvivable.
A person who never learned to ask for comfort directly may state the feeling in its most extreme form.
Alcohol or exhaustion can turn sadness into something louder late at night.
common_false_positives: A friend confiding that they have thought about ending their life, which is a disclosure and not a demand.
A teenager who says 'I want to die' about an embarrassing moment and laughs. It still deserves a gentle check, but it is not a lever.
A partner in treatment who tells you they are having a bad week and wants you to know.
discernment_questions: Does the statement come with a request about what I should do, or with a request for help?
When I suggested a counselor, a crisis line or a relative, was that accepted or pushed aside?
Has my own plan, such as seeing a friend or taking a job, changed more than once because of these statements?
Do I feel I am the only person who knows, and the only one who can keep them safe?
Who outside this situation could help me tell fear for them apart from being steered?
less_concerning_if: The distress is shared on ordinary days, with no demand tied to it.
They take up professional or family help when it is offered.
Your choices have stayed your own even while they struggle.
more_concerning_if: The statements come with a plan, a method close at hand, a recent attempt or goodbye messages. That needs urgent help whatever else is going on.
The threats grow more frequent or more specific as your independence grows.
They also monitor you, turn up unannounced or physically block you when you try to go.
pattern_over_time_signs: You have stopped saying plans out loud, in case the answer turns into a crisis.
You carry your phone everywhere and check it in the middle of events, afraid of missing a message.
Friends and family see less of you because evenings keep being cut short.
You feel guilty about ordinary things, like switching your phone off to sleep.
Self-Harm Threats as Leverage.repair_check: The plan does not run through you alone: a clinician, a written safety plan, a relative they trust, and the person actually using them when they struggle. Repair also means they can hear 'no' on an ordinary day without the subject returning to their life or death. Tearful apologies alone do not show it.
Self-Harm Threats as Leverage.boundary_respect_check: Notice whether your wish to bring in a third person is welcomed or fought. When someone is in danger from their own thoughts, an extra helper often brings relief. If every route except you gets refused, that is worth noting, privately and with someone you trust.
Self-Harm Threats as Leverage.psychological_mechanism: Threats like this can fuse two fears: that the person will die, and that you will be the cause. Compassion and responsibility are strong, and once one choice is framed as life or death, weighing your own needs can seem cruel. The effect can outlast the crisis, since you learn that a no may carry a price.
Self-Harm Threats as Leverage.possible_impact_on_receiver: Constant alertness comes up often, as does a sense of being responsible for another adult's life, plans dropped to stay near the phone, and guilt whether you stay or step away. Numbness is reported, or relief mixed with shame once a crisis passes. Many kept it secret in case the person got into trouble.

response_options.soft_clarification: Stay with the feeling first: 'I can hear how much pain you're in, and I take it seriously.' Then ask the plain question: 'Are you thinking of hurting yourself tonight?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold that you are one support and not the only one: 'I care about you, and I can't be the only thing keeping you safe. Let's call a crisis line together.'
response_options.disengagement: If a threat arrives while you are apart, you do not have to argue it out by text. Send a crisis number, or ask a relative nearby to check in on them, and keep your own reply short and kind.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell one person you trust what was said, in the actual words, and ask a counselor or a domestic abuse advocate how to respond. You should not carry this by yourself.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If the messages arrive during work hours, you can tell a manager you have a personal emergency without giving detail, and ask whether your employer offers a counseling program.

Self-Harm Threats as Leverage.boundary_script: "I believe it hurts, and I'm taking what you said seriously. I can't be the only one who helps you stay safe, so I'd like us to call a crisis line together right now. Would it help if I rang your brother to come over?"
Self-Harm Threats as Leverage.safety_note: Any talk of suicide deserves a real response, whatever lies behind it. Danger signs are a stated plan, a method at hand, a recent attempt or goodbye messages. If you see them, contact local emergency services or a crisis line (988 in the United States) on their behalf. Separately, if the threats rise whenever you try to be independent, an advocate can help you plan privately. Your next step is to bring in one outside helper.
misuse_warning: Do not treat every expression of despair as manipulation. If you cannot tell which it is, treat it as real danger and get help; the pattern can be sorted out later.
Telling others that someone was 'only threatening' can leave a person who is in real crisis without help.
Self-Harm Threats as Leverage.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Emotional Blackmail attaches many possible losses, such as withdrawn love, exposure or anger, to a refusal; here the stake is the speaker's own life. Pity Plays end in comfort and a change of subject, but they do not tie your decision to survival. Guilt-Tripping stays with blame and conscience and holds no threat of actual harm. This is the entry where your choice is linked to whether someone lives.

Pity Plays.short_definition: Answering a concern with displays of helplessness or victimhood, so the person who raised it ends up offering comfort and the concern is dropped.
Pity Plays.core_meaning: Answering a concern with displays of helplessness or victimhood, so the person who raised it ends up offering comfort and the concern is dropped.
Pity Plays.expanded_definition: Pity plays are moments when a complaint, a question or a request for change is answered with collapse: tears, 'nobody loves me', 'I'm hopeless at everything'. The original subject gets lost as the person who raised it moves into comforting. Real pain can look exactly the same, and one tearful night after a hard conversation proves nothing. Timing is what counts. The distress appears at the moment of accountability, the issue is not returned to, and over time bringing anything up begins to seem cruel.
Pity Plays.plain_language_summary: You bring up something that bothered you, and the conversation turns into you reassuring them. The original problem never gets looked at.
Pity Plays.why_this_matters: When every concern ends in reassurance, the problem stays where it was and your need to be heard shrinks. Over time you may stop raising things at all, which makes the relationship quieter but no more honest.
what_it_is: A reaction that grows as the complaint gets more specific: a calm 'you forgot' meets sobbing, silence or 'I'm a terrible person'.
Sweeping statements about oneself, like 'I always ruin things', that are too large to answer, so comfort is the only reply left.
A swap of roles in mid-conversation: the person who raised the issue is soon the one hugging, apologising or backing down.
A topic that is not picked up again once the person has calmed.
Seen between partners, but also parents and adult children, friends and coworkers.
what_it_sounds_like: Fine, I'm just a terrible friend. Everyone's better off without me.
You'd abandon me too, like everyone else.
I can't do anything right, can I.
After the week I've had, this is what you bring up?
I'm always the bad guy, aren't I.
Look at me, I'm shaking. Are you happy now?
Never mind. I'll stop talking about anything.
what_it_is_not: Depression or low self-worth speaking, which shows up outside conflict too and calls for care.
Someone overwhelmed by shame who cries and goes quiet, then comes back the next day and talks it through.
A grieving or exhausted person who truly cannot have the conversation tonight and says so plainly.
A person who says 'that hurts to hear' and then listens to the rest.
A family style of speaking in strong emotional terms about everything, not only when challenged.
A request for comfort in a moment unrelated to anything you asked of them.
this_may_be_it_when: Distress rises sharply when you ask for a specific change and is absent on neutral topics.
Their statements about themselves are global ('always', 'never', 'everyone') and not about the incident.
Your original point is not mentioned again, and you are the one who apologises.
Comfort is needed until they are visibly better, with the concern still unresolved.
A similar scene has followed each time you raised something about the same issue.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They cry, then say 'I want to come back to what you said', and do.
Their sadness is about something else entirely, and they ask for support for that alone.
The distress fits the size of what happened, and the concern still gets addressed.
They show the same vulnerability when nobody has asked anything of them.
They accept 'I can listen to you and still need to talk about this' without a further collapse.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Criticism lands on some people as a verdict on their whole worth, so tears come before thoughts.
Someone raised in a home where mistakes brought anger may freeze or collapse when told of one.
Tiredness, grief or illness can make an ordinary complaint hit much harder than usual.
Some people can only process by crying first and talking second.
common_false_positives: A friend who breaks down after hard feedback, then thanks you the next day and makes the change.
A relative with ongoing depression who says bleak things in all kinds of conversations.
A young child who dissolves into tears after being corrected, which is development and not performance.
discernment_questions: After I raised the concern, did we ever go back to it?
Is the sadness about what happened, or about the fact that I said something?
Do I leave these conversations having apologised or comforted, with nothing resolved?
Do they show the same low moments on days when I have asked for nothing?
Have I stopped mentioning things because I know how it will go?
less_concerning_if: The low feeling is spoken about in general, not only when you ask for something.
The original concern is picked up again once the emotion settles.
They can tell you what they need, such as an hour, and then come back.
more_concerning_if: You now check your words in advance to avoid setting off a collapse.
Concerns about money, safety or health stay unresolved because every scene ends in comfort.
Other people who raise concerns with them describe the same scene.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your list of unspoken concerns keeps growing.
You have become the manager of their moods.
Disagreements get shorter because you drop your point early.
You think of them as fragile and of yourself as the sturdy one, with no room to be upset.
Pity Plays.repair_check: What counts is whether the dropped concern comes back. Once they have steadied, they open with it themselves: 'I want to go back to what you said about the money.' Reassurance in the moment, with no later return to the subject, leaves the pattern where it was.
Pity Plays.boundary_respect_check: Ask yourself: when I say 'I care how you feel, and I still need an answer', does one arrive within a day or two? Watch whether the answer eventually comes, or whether each attempt starts the same scene again.
Pity Plays.psychological_mechanism: Most people are quick to soothe someone who is crying, and that instinct tends to fire before we have thought about what we were saying. Visible distress can move attention from the concern to the person's wellbeing, and raise doubt about whether you had the right to speak. Repeated, this can teach the one raising concerns that doing so causes harm.
Pity Plays.possible_impact_on_receiver: Conversations become careful: complaints get softened in advance, speaking up brings a flash of cruelty, and talks end with you more drained than when they started. Doubt creeps in about whether your concerns were fair. Resentment can build quietly over issues nobody answered, followed by guilt for feeling it.

response_options.soft_clarification: Hold both things aloud: 'I can see you're hurting, and I still need us to finish talking about this.' Offer a break with a time to return, such as tomorrow evening.
response_options.firm_boundary: Name the loop gently and stay on the subject: 'When I raise something, we end up talking about how you feel and never about what I said. I'd like us to do both.'
response_options.disengagement: Comfort them briefly, then step out of the room until the emotion has settled, and bring the topic back the next day in a short conversation or message.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe two recent scenes to a friend or counselor and ask whether your concerns were reasonable. It is hard to tell from inside, since the distress is real.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, put the concern in an email with a specific request and a date, so it does not depend on how a conversation goes, and ask a manager to attend if talks keep stalling.

Pity Plays.boundary_script: "I can see how much this hurts, and I'm not trying to make it worse. I also need us to talk about what I raised. Take as long as you need, and we'll pick it up tomorrow after dinner."
Pity Plays.safety_note: Pity plays on their own are not usually a danger signal. What would change that is distress that turns into threats against yourself or them, or into monitoring and blocking contact when you step away. If the sadness ever comes with talk of ending their life, treat that as its own matter and read the entry on self-harm threats. A first step is to write down, privately, which concerns are still unanswered.
misuse_warning: Tears are not proof of a tactic. Calling real grief a 'pity play' can dismiss the pain of someone who is genuinely struggling.
Take care with this label for a person with depression or a trauma history, whose distress may be entirely sincere and who may still need the conversation to happen later.
Pity Plays.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Martyrdom Display advertises sacrifice already made ('after all I do'), while pity plays voice present helplessness and the exchange ends in comfort. Self-Harm Threats tie a choice of yours to the speaker's survival; pity plays express hopelessness without a link to what you decide. Guilt-Tripping blames you for a harm, whereas here the speaker is the one harmed. The difference is which story takes the stage: your concern, or their suffering.

Martyrdom Display.short_definition: Pointing out one's own unrewarded effort and sacrifice in a way that leaves the other person feeling indebted and unable to say no.
Martyrdom Display.core_meaning: Pointing out one's own unrewarded effort and sacrifice in a way that leaves the other person feeling indebted and unable to say no.
Martyrdom Display.expanded_definition: Martyrdom display is the habit of making effort and self-denial visible: the sighs, the 'don't mind me', the list of what has been given up. Help is not asked for directly. Instead the sacrifice sits in the room until someone offers to fix it. One tired remark after a long week is ordinary. The pattern is the same scene each time help is wanted, and a running debt that grows whether or not you agreed to the cost.
Martyrdom Display.plain_language_summary: Someone makes their sacrifices obvious instead of asking for help, so you feel you owe them. A plain request would have been easier to answer.
Martyrdom Display.why_this_matters: A debt you never agreed to is hard to pay, because the total keeps changing. You may give more time or help than you wanted and then resent it, while the real need for support never gets spoken.
what_it_is: Doing a task loudly, with clattering dishes or heavy sighs, so the effort is seen though nobody asked for it.
Turning down help with 'no, I'll do it', then reminding you later that nobody helped.
Keeping a mental ledger of sacrifices and bringing out entries in unrelated arguments.
Avoiding a direct request for what is needed, so the only answer open to you is to offer.
Found in families, workplaces, caregiving and partnerships where one person does more of the visible work.
what_it_sounds_like: Don't mind me, I'll sit here alone.
I guess I'll just do it myself like always.
I gave up my whole twenties for this family, but sure, go.
No, no, go and enjoy yourself. I'll be fine with the dishes.
I haven't sat down since six this morning. Not that anyone noticed.
I'd never ask you for anything.
Twelve hours on my feet, and I'm not complaining.
what_it_is_not: Honest tiredness said once, such as 'I'm worn out tonight', that asks you to do nothing.
Someone who truly carries an unfair load and is clumsily trying to say so. They may need a better way to ask, not a label.
A direct request: 'I'm overloaded. Could you do the school run on Thursdays?'
A caregiver describing the facts of their week to a friend who asked.
A person who gives generously and does not mention it or expect a return.
A team meeting where everyone lists what they have finished.
this_may_be_it_when: Offers of help are refused, and then the lack of help is mentioned.
The sacrifice is listed just as you are about to do something for yourself.
No direct request has been made, yet you feel you must offer.
The same phrases come back in many different situations.
Your decision to say no is met with days of silence or sighing, and not with a conversation.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They accept help gladly when it is offered and say thank you.
They ask for what they need in a single sentence.
The effort is mentioned once, and nothing in their tone expects a reply.
They are happy for you to go out and do not make you pay for it later.
They are able to say no to other people as well.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Some people learned in childhood that asking for help brings rejection, so they hint and hope.
In some families, quiet self-sacrifice is how love is shown, and mentioning it is how it gets said.
Exhaustion can make a person say more than they mean, and the words land like a bill.
A person may truly not know how to ask, and think that mentioning the work is the same as asking.
common_false_positives: A friend who says 'I'm wiped, I've been up with the baby' and expects nothing in return.
A relative who quietly does a great deal of unpaid caring and is not acknowledged by the rest of the family.
A coworker who lists what they have finished at a stand-up meeting.
discernment_questions: If I offered help right now, would it be accepted?
Was a direct request ever made, or have I been left to guess?
Is the sacrifice mentioned when I am about to do something I want?
Do I feel I owe something I never agreed to carry?
Is there a genuinely uneven load here that I could see without being shown it?
less_concerning_if: The tiredness is mentioned and followed by a simple request.
Help, when given, is thanked and then forgotten.
The person can say how much they have done without it turning into what you owe.
more_concerning_if: A refusal is followed by days of coldness or sighing.
Past sacrifices are brought up when you raise unrelated needs of your own.
The total owed seems to rise whatever you give.
pattern_over_time_signs: You volunteer for tasks before being asked, to avoid the sighs.
You feel a flicker of dread before telling them your plans.
Your own plans shrink to the ones that are easy to defend.
You resent someone you also feel sorry for.
Martyrdom Display.repair_check: Watch what happens to the requests. A change looks like a plain 'I need help with Saturday', help accepted without commentary, and a refusal received without days of quiet. Thanks for one day's help followed by sighing through the next refusal has not changed the part that matters.
Martyrdom Display.boundary_respect_check: Try a small test: say yes to part of a request and no to the rest. Notice whether the part you gave is received with thanks or with a list of what you did not do. The reaction to the 'no' says more than the reaction to the 'yes'.
Martyrdom Display.psychological_mechanism: Visible sacrifice creates a felt debt without any request, and since nothing was asked, there is nothing to refuse. Reciprocity is a strong social habit, and owing something is uncomfortable. With no direct request to answer, a no lands as turning down a plea that was never spoken.
Martyrdom Display.possible_impact_on_receiver: Guilt with no clear source, a sense of never doing enough, help offered out of dread more than willingness, and resentment that then brings its own shame are all reported. Avoidance follows for some: dreading holidays and chores because even kind acts seemed to add to the tally.

response_options.soft_clarification: Turn the hint into a request you can answer: 'It sounds like a lot is on you. What would help most this week?' Then do what you can, and say what you cannot.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline the debt, not the person: 'I'm happy to do Thursdays. I won't take on the rest because of how the week has looked.'
response_options.disengagement: When the sighing starts, you can leave the room or change the subject without trying to repair the mood, and carry on with the plan you had.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask a sibling, friend or counselor whether the split of work in your household looks fair from outside, and what a fair split might be.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, bring workload questions to the team in a shared list with names and hours, so effort is visible to everyone and not held as private leverage.

Martyrdom Display.boundary_script: "I can see you've been doing a lot, and I want to help in a way that works for both of us. I can take Thursdays. I can't take on everything just because it's been hard. Can we write down who does what?"
Martyrdom Display.safety_note: Martyrdom display on its own carries no particular danger. What would change that is sacrifice used to control where you go, whom you see or how you spend money, or any hint of retaliation when you decline. If that appears, write down specific examples and talk to a counselor or advocate before changing the arrangement. A practical first step is a written split of tasks.
misuse_warning: A person who really does carry far more than their share may sound like this when worn out. Calling it a tactic can excuse everyone else from the work.
Be careful with the label for elders and carers, whose self-sacrifice is often real and unseen.
Martyrdom Display.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Pity Plays focus on present helplessness and end in comfort; martyrdom display lists sacrifices already made and ends in owing. Demand for Gratitude asks outright for thanks after help, while martyrdom display usually asks for nothing aloud and lets the effort speak. Guilt-Tripping blames you for something you did, whereas here the claim is about what the speaker has done for you. The difference is a ledger of the speaker's effort, kept in view but never itemised as a bill.

Duty Scripts.short_definition: Using a role such as daughter, son or parent as an unarguable rule for what one must do, so refusing sounds like failing at the role.
Duty Scripts.core_meaning: Using a role such as daughter, son or parent as an unarguable rule for what one must do, so refusing sounds like failing at the role.
Duty Scripts.expanded_definition: Duty scripts take a family or social role and turn it into a rulebook that only one person gets to read. 'A good daughter would...' leaves no space to ask whether the role really requires this, or whether it is the speaker's place to judge. Values about family and respect are real and deeply held in many cultures, so invoking one is not the problem. The pattern is the role used to end a discussion: the request is not argued on its merits, and saying no is treated as a failure of who you are.
Duty Scripts.plain_language_summary: Someone says what a good son, daughter, parent or friend would do, and the request stops being a request. Saying no starts to look like a flaw in you.
Duty Scripts.why_this_matters: When 'what a good daughter does' replaces 'what do you think', your own judgment about your life is outranked by a rule you did not write. People can lose track of what they want, and the relationship starts to feel like a test they can fail.
what_it_is: A request dressed as a rule about a role: 'a good son visits', 'a mother's word is final'.
A definition of the role that only the speaker may set and that can shift to fit the request.
Arguments that skip the practical questions (can you, is it fair?) and go straight to what kind of person you are.
Often tied to family hierarchy, age, culture or religion, though not unique to any of them.
Heard at weddings, caregiving crises, inheritance talks and holidays, when a family is deciding who does what.
what_it_sounds_like: A good daughter would never say that.
Family comes first. You owe us this.
I didn't raise you to talk back to your father.
It's your duty as the eldest.
You're a mother now. Your own plans don't count.
Because I am your mother, that's why.
A real friend would have been there.
Who's going to look after her if not you?
what_it_is_not: A family or cultural value stated as one consideration, with room to say 'I see it differently' and still be loved.
An honest 'we are counting on you for Sunday', which names a need and accepts a no.
A relative sharing what duty meant to their own generation without requiring the same of you.
Obligations you chose, such as caring for your child or keeping a promise, where the duty is plain and shared.
Religious or community teaching about duty given in a sermon or lesson, not aimed at a particular decision.
A parent setting house rules for a young child.
this_may_be_it_when: Your reasons for declining are never answered, only the role you are failing.
The meaning of the role shifts to fit each new request.
Siblings who hold the same role are not held to the same standard.
The phrase is used at the moment you try to decide something for yourself.
A question like 'what do you think?' would feel out of place in the conversation.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They ask about your situation and adjust.
Several people share the duty equally.
The expectation was known when you took on the role, and applies to the speaker too.
You can say 'I can't do this one' and the relationship stays warm.
The talk of duty is about the speaker's own choices and not yours.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many families express love through duty language, and those may be the only words available.
Someone worried about an ageing parent may reach for the strongest phrase they know.
A speaker may truly believe the rule they quote and be repeating what was said to them.
common_false_positives: A parent telling a seven-year-old that in this house we say thank you.
A sibling saying 'we all agreed to split Mum's care', reminding you of a commitment you made.
A faith leader teaching about family responsibility to the whole congregation.
discernment_questions: Who defined this role, and was I ever asked?
Do the same expectations apply to the people saying this?
Does the speaker want to hear my reasons, or only whether I will comply?
If the request had been made as a request, would I have said yes?
Am I being judged by a rulebook I could not have read in advance?
less_concerning_if: The expectation is open to discussion, and you can say what you are able to give.
The speaker holds themselves to the same rule.
Duty is mentioned as a value and not used at the moment of a decision.
more_concerning_if: Declining brings exclusion from family events or being spoken of as a disgrace.
The role is used to control your education, relationships, money or where you live.
Other relatives are asked to enforce the script and pass on its judgments.
pattern_over_time_signs: You hear the script in your own head when you think of saying no.
You decide things by asking what you are supposed to do, not what you want.
You feel something close to shame at ordinary boundaries.
You have stopped telling certain relatives your plans until they are settled.
Duty Scripts.repair_check: Start with whether the role stops being the argument. A shift would sound like 'what do you think you can manage?', with the rule left out, and a refusal that leaves your standing in the family unchanged. A warm apology followed by 'a good son would' at the next decision has changed only the tone.
Duty Scripts.boundary_respect_check: Notice what changes after you say 'I can't do that, and I am still your daughter.' Is your place at the table the same? Pay attention to whether invitations, calls and warmth continue, or whether something quietly goes cold.
Duty Scripts.psychological_mechanism: Roles carry heavy moral weight, and many people take on their family's idea of a good son, daughter or parent early in life. With a request attached to that identity, refusing registers as failing at who you are, not as choosing between options. The rule is never written down, so it cannot be checked, and it can stretch to cover new situations.
Duty Scripts.possible_impact_on_receiver: Being split between what the family expects and what you want is the usual report, along with deciding like a child would and carrying shame at choosing for yourself. Some could not tell what they wanted for years. Others are left with distance from relatives they love, and grief at what saying no has cost.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask which part of the request matters most, and what the person is most worried about: 'Tell me what you need on Sunday, and I'll tell you what I can do.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Separate the role from the request: 'I am your daughter, and I can't take this on. Please ask me as a question, not as a rule.'
response_options.disengagement: When the script begins, say you will talk about the practical side later and move to another topic, without defending what a good daughter does.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk to someone outside the family who respects your background, such as a cousin, a faith counselor or a therapist familiar with your culture, about where duty ends and pressure starts.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, when a role like 'team player' is used to justify unpaid extras, ask what the written duties are and answer the request in terms of hours and scope.

Duty Scripts.boundary_script: "I take being a good son seriously, and that is why I'm being honest that I can't do this one. It isn't that I don't care about the family. The answer is no. Let's talk about what I can do instead."
Duty Scripts.safety_note: Role pressure is usually painful rather than dangerous. It changes when refusing brings threats, confiscated phones or papers, being kept in, a forced marriage or travel plan, or talk of family honor tied to harm. Those call for specialist help, such as a forced marriage or domestic abuse service, or legal aid. A first step is to find that service quietly, before any family conversation.
misuse_warning: Cultural or religious duty is not itself a form of pressure. Applying this label to a whole family's values dismisses traditions many people hold dear.
A relative saying 'family comes first' may be asking, not scripting. Check for the pattern before naming it.
Duty Scripts.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Guilt-Tripping blames you for a harm already done, while duty scripts rest on a role you hold, so the claim is about who you are supposed to be. Emotional Blackmail attaches a loss, such as love or approval, to a decision; duty scripts need no threat, only the role's authority. Demand for Gratitude says you owe thanks for help given, but duty scripts say you owe compliance because of a bond. The difference is where the authority is claimed: a rulebook of roles, not a record of acts.

Demand for Gratitude.short_definition: Expecting thanks on demand, in the right words or amount, as the price of help given, so that generosity ends up with conditions attached.
Demand for Gratitude.core_meaning: Expecting thanks on demand, in the right words or amount, as the price of help given, so that generosity ends up with conditions attached.
Demand for Gratitude.expanded_definition: Demand for gratitude turns help into something that must be repaid in visible thanks. The help may be real: a lift, a loan, a roof, a favor. What changes is that thanks is asked for, measured and chased. A single 'a thank-you would be nice' after a long day is a human feeling. Look for thanks that must come in particular forms, gratitude raised again weeks later, and a helped person made to feel lower for having been helped.
Demand for Gratitude.plain_language_summary: You were helped, and now you are expected to keep showing how thankful you are, in the right way, or be reminded of it. Help turns into a cost.
Demand for Gratitude.why_this_matters: When thanks is required, help stops being a gift and starts to feel like a loan with interest. People can start to avoid accepting help, even when they need it, or hide small wins so nobody feels unappreciated.
what_it_is: Thanks asked for out loud ('Where's my thank you?') or counted ('You only said it once').
A specific form demanded, such as a card, a public mention, a visit or a particular tone.
A change of mood when thanks seems too small: a cooler voice, a shorter visit, a withdrawn offer.
Help given in a way that makes the amount of thanks owed obvious, with a mention of cost, effort or time.
Seen between parents and adult children, hosts and guests, employers and workers, and friends.
what_it_sounds_like: A thank-you would be nice for once.
After everything I did to get you that job, not even a card?
I'm still waiting to hear thank you.
You said thanks, but you didn't sound like you meant it.
Other people would be on their knees thanking me.
I don't ask for much. Just a little appreciation.
Did you thank her properly? Look how much she's done for you.
what_it_is_not: Hurt feelings that help went unmentioned, said once and kindly: 'It would mean a lot to hear that it helped.'
Teaching a child to say please and thank you, a normal part of manners.
A charity or club that thanks donors publicly, with the acknowledgement agreed in advance.
Close friends who say thanks for small things as a habit both of them enjoy.
A person who gave a great deal, is worn thin and wants to be seen, which is different from wanting to be repaid.
A workplace that recognizes effort in a review.
this_may_be_it_when: The thanks is checked afterwards: how it was said, when, and in front of whom.
A thank-you from you has to be repeated or made bigger to count.
Not thanking in the preferred way is met with a cooler tone or less help afterwards.
Help arrives with a mention of what it cost, before you have said anything.
You receive reminders of your ingratitude weeks after the help.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They say 'you're welcome' and move on.
They said they were hurt once and did not need it repeated or performed.
Help continues on the same terms whether you thank them loudly, quietly or not at all.
Both of you can say thanks and receive it with ease.
They say the help came with no strings and behave that way.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People who rarely received thanks growing up may feel its absence sharply.
A busy, tired helper may ask for acknowledgement simply because it has been a long week.
Cultures differ in how much thanks is expected, and what looks cold in one looks polite in another.
Receivers often forget to say thanks in a crisis, and the helper's hurt is then genuine.
common_false_positives: A parent reminding a teenager to thank their grandmother for a gift.
A friend who says 'I felt unseen when I helped you move, and wanted you to know.'
A group where each member sends thanks after a shared meal as an agreed custom.
discernment_questions: Was this help offered freely, or did it come with expectations I did not hear?
Is the thanks I give ever enough, or does the bar keep moving?
What happens when I do not show gratitude in the way they expected?
Do I keep up the thanks because I feel it, or because I fear what happens if I stop?
Would I still accept this help if I knew how much repayment it carried?
less_concerning_if: A wish to hear thanks is stated once, kindly, and does not return.
The helper stays warm when thanks is brief or late.
Help is offered again later on the same terms.
more_concerning_if: Thanks is demanded in front of other people, or in a way that embarrasses you.
Help is withdrawn, or threatened, when thanks falls short.
The help being held up as owed is a basic such as housing, rides or money.
pattern_over_time_signs: You over-thank, or rehearse your thank-yous, to avoid friction.
You hide good news or skip asking for help to stay out of debt.
You flinch at a gift, wondering what it will cost.
Visits and calls start to feel like repayments.
Demand for Gratitude.repair_check: The moment thanks arrives shows it. A shift sounds like a simple 'glad I could help', then no follow-up check, and a later offer given without a reminder. Another speech about how much has been done, even a warm one, keeps the meter running.
Demand for Gratitude.boundary_respect_check: Tell them you are grateful and that you would like help between you to be given freely or not at all. Then see how the next offer arrives: with fewer conditions, or with a longer reminder of the last one?
Demand for Gratitude.psychological_mechanism: Gratitude is a real and valuable feeling, and most people want to repay kindness. When thanks is demanded, that feeling can be treated as a payment due, and a person who is slow to produce it may feel ungenerous. Because the amount owed is never fixed, the debt rarely feels settled, and staying quietly agreeable can seem easier.
Demand for Gratitude.possible_impact_on_receiver: Never having thanked enough is a frequent feeling, with discomfort at accepting gifts, rehearsed thank-yous, and hiding anything that might look ungrateful. Asking for help can stop altogether, since it would add to the account. A slow dislike can grow toward someone the person has real reason to appreciate.

response_options.soft_clarification: Offer thanks that is true and specific: 'The lift got me to the interview on time, and I appreciated it.' Then notice whether it lands, or whether more is expected.
response_options.firm_boundary: Tell them the way thanks is being asked for is hard for you: 'I am grateful, and I can't be asked for it every time we talk.'
response_options.disengagement: If a meeting turns into a review of your gratitude, close that part with one 'thank you again' and move on, without adding more.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask a friend, relative or counselor whether help like this would normally come with this much accounting, or whether you are missing something.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a manager or mentor keeps referring to what they did for your career, thank them once in writing, then keep the working relationship on tasks and agreements.

Demand for Gratitude.boundary_script: "What you did mattered, and I mean that. I'd like help between us to work without a scorecard. If it comes with a need for more thanks, I would rather manage on my own."
Demand for Gratitude.safety_note: Demand for gratitude is not usually dangerous in itself. The picture changes when the help is housing, money or papers and thanks becomes a condition of keeping them, or when refusing brings a threat of being put out. In that case, quietly look up tenant advice, legal aid or a relevant advocate before changing the arrangement, and keep copies of anything that is yours.
misuse_warning: Wanting appreciation is human. Using this label every time someone mentions that they helped would silence honest feelings.
Do not apply it to a child learning manners, or to someone who was truly not thanked after a big effort.
Demand for Gratitude.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Martyrdom Display shows sacrifice through sighs and 'don't mind me' and asks for nothing aloud; demand for gratitude names the thanks it expects. Duty Scripts claim you owe obedience because of a role, while here you owe acknowledgement because of help given. Guilt-Tripping makes you feel at fault for a harm, and demand for gratitude makes you feel at fault for not feeling thankful enough. The difference is the object: your thanks, in a particular form, as the thing being collected.

Favor Debt.short_definition: Citing past gifts, money or support as the reason someone must agree to a present request, so past kindness is treated like a signed contract.
Favor Debt.core_meaning: Citing past gifts, money or support as the reason someone must agree to a present request, so past kindness is treated like a signed contract.
Favor Debt.expanded_definition: Favor debt is the habit of citing what one has given, such as school fees, a loan, a place to stay or a favor, as the reason you must say yes to something now. Mutual support is part of nearly every close relationship, and mentioning it is not a problem. The pattern is when old help becomes a lever on a particular decision, can be cited again and again, and has no end point: whatever you give, the balance stays open.
Favor Debt.plain_language_summary: Someone reminds you of everything they gave you and uses it to get a yes now. Whatever you do, the balance never seems paid off.
Favor Debt.why_this_matters: A debt you never agreed to has no settlement date, so you can be asked to pay it over and over. People may stay in jobs, relationships or cities they would have left, or hand over money they cannot spare, because refusing feels like taking from someone who helped.
what_it_is: A past gift or support used as the reason for a present request: 'After I paid your rent, you can do this.'
A balance that is never closed: whatever you give back, the original help is still cited.
Help given earlier and described afterwards as a loan, though nobody said so at the time.
Covers money, favors, time, introductions, housing or a career opening.
Found in families, friendships, workplaces and partnerships where one person has more resources.
what_it_sounds_like: Remember who paid for your school.
You owe me after everything.
Everything you have is because of me.
I put a roof over your head when nobody else would.
Who do you think got you that interview?
I covered your rent for a year. The least you can do is cover for me.
After what I spent on your wedding, you can host us.
what_it_is_not: A friend saying 'I lent you money in March, can we talk about when you might pay it back?', which is an openly agreed loan.
Mutual support in a long relationship mentioned honestly: 'We have always helped each other.'
A request for help after helping, offered as a request that accepts a no.
A written agreement to repay, such as a mortgage or family loan, and a reminder of its terms.
A parent saying once, while sad, what they gave up for a child, with no demand attached.
Proper credit within a team for work that helped you.
this_may_be_it_when: Help from years ago is cited when you are asked for something today.
No terms of repayment were stated at the time, but now there are some.
Whatever you do to give back is called too little.
A reminder of the debt arrives at the moment you hesitate.
Declining a request is treated as ingratitude toward the person who helped.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Terms of repayment were agreed at the time, in words or writing.
The helper says 'you owe me nothing' and acts that way when you decline.
Both of you have helped each other, and either can ask.
Your 'no' is accepted without a reminder.
The debt is a plain sum with an end.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Someone who helped at real cost may feel hurt when things now seem one-sided.
People under financial strain may remember exactly who gave what, because every pound counts.
Some families treat generosity as a loan that is expected to come back, and see that as normal.
A person may mention past help to explain why they are asking, with no thought of compelling you.
common_false_positives: A sibling who repaid you last month and now asks for a return favor, describing the arrangement as mutual.
A mentor who asks you once to help a new employee as they helped you, and takes a no kindly.
A friend who mentions a past loan because they are short this month and wants to agree a repayment plan.
discernment_questions: Were there terms when the help was given, or did they appear later?
Is this a request I can decline, or has it been framed as something I cannot?
Does anything I give back ever count as enough?
Does the reminder arrive whenever I hesitate over something unrelated to the original help?
Does help run in both directions in this relationship?
less_concerning_if: Earlier help is mentioned as context while the current request stays optional.
A repayment has been named, and it can be completed.
Both sides can count what the other has done without turning it against each other.
more_concerning_if: The debt is used on decisions about your own life: where you live, whom you marry, what job you take.
Money is involved and your name is on loans, accounts or papers you did not choose.
Saying no brings a cut-off of help you depend on, such as housing, tuition or childcare.
pattern_over_time_signs: You track what you have been given and feel a sting when the person is generous again.
You turn down help you need, to avoid being in someone's debt.
You have said yes to requests you would rather have refused, simply to settle the balance.
The list of what you owe keeps growing, though nothing new has been given.
Favor Debt.repair_check: A different pattern shows up as terms: help is named as a gift, or as a loan with a sum and a date, and past help stops being cited when you decline something. A change of tone followed by the same reminder at the next 'no' leaves the account open.
Favor Debt.boundary_respect_check: Ask whether the debt can be named and closed. If you offer to repay a specific sum or to thank them in a specific way, notice whether they accept it as settled. A reaction that raises the amount, or keeps the sum vague, tells you the account cannot be closed from your side.
Favor Debt.psychological_mechanism: A strong pull to return favors is useful in healthy relationships. When help is later described as a debt, that sense of fairness can be pointed at a request with no link to the original help. The sum is never fixed, so repaying is never finished, and refusing can seem like taking from someone who gave.
Favor Debt.possible_impact_on_receiver: Being trapped by one's own history is a common report, along with avoiding gifts for fear of the cost and agreeing to things disliked just to quiet the reminder. The mix is often bitter: real gratitude alongside anger. Some stayed in a place or a job longer than they wanted.

response_options.soft_clarification: Acknowledge the help and ask to separate it from the request: 'I'm grateful for what you did for my schooling. Can we talk about this request on its own?'
response_options.firm_boundary: State that thanks and agreement are different things: 'I will always appreciate what you did. That doesn't mean I can say yes to this.'
response_options.disengagement: When the reminder comes, you can decline to go through the list again and return to the question in front of you, or end the call.
response_options.support_seeking: Write down what was given and what was agreed at the time, and take it to a friend, an accountant or a legal aid adviser if money or property is involved.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a mentor or boss cites past favors, ask for any commitments in writing and keep decisions about your role tied to your duties, not to who sponsored your career.

Favor Debt.boundary_script: "I haven't forgotten what you did for me, and I'm still grateful. I can't pay it back by agreeing to this one. Tell me a way to thank you that I can really do."
Favor Debt.safety_note: Favor debt becomes a safety matter when the debt is financial or legal: loans in your name, a sponsored visa or housing tied to compliance, or threats to cut off what you depend on. Keep copies of any papers you have signed, and get independent advice from legal aid or a tenant or immigration adviser before changing anything.
misuse_warning: Mentioning past help is not always a lever. Calling every reminder of support 'favor debt' can brush aside people who really did give a lot and are asking fairly.
Do not use the label to avoid repaying a loan that was clearly agreed.
Favor Debt.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Duty Scripts rest on a role (a good son would) and need no past act; favor debt rests on something that was actually given, such as fees or rent. Emotional Blackmail threatens a loss of love or approval if you refuse, while favor debt points back at what has already been provided. Guilt-Tripping blames you for a hurt you caused, but favor debt claims you are in arrears for a kindness. The difference is the ledger: a specific past gift cited as payment due now.

Catastrophizing as Control.short_definition: Predicting that someone will fall into ruin, loneliness or disaster if they act independently, so that leaving or choosing differently begins to feel unsafe.
Catastrophizing as Control.core_meaning: Predicting that someone will fall into ruin, loneliness or disaster if they act independently, so that leaving or choosing differently begins to feel unsafe.
Catastrophizing as Control.expanded_definition: Catastrophizing as control means painting the future in worst-case terms whenever the other person is about to make a choice of their own: a job, a move, a friendship, an end to the relationship. The predictions come as facts, not worries, and they usually cast the speaker as the one thing keeping disaster away. Worry about someone you love is normal, and a frank warning can be a kindness. The pattern is predictions that outsize the real risk, return at each step toward independence, and leave you less able to trust your own plans.
Catastrophizing as Control.plain_language_summary: When you move toward something of your own, someone predicts you will end up broke, alone or ruined without them, until managing alone feels impossible.
Catastrophizing as Control.why_this_matters: Fear of the future can keep a person in place more firmly than any rule. When every independent step is described as the start of ruin, you may stop trying, stay where you are, and lose confidence that you could cope.
what_it_is: Forecasts of disaster delivered as certainties: 'you will lose the house', not 'I am worried about the house'.
A prediction that you personally will fail without the speaker, whatever the plan is.
Disaster linked to many different choices: a job, a course, a move, a friend, a decision to leave.
A forecast that does not change when you show a plan, savings or support.
Sometimes passed through others ('your mother is frightened for you') or backed by selected stories of people who failed.
what_it_sounds_like: If you take that job, this family falls apart.
You'll end up alone and broke without me.
No one else will put up with you the way I do.
You can't survive out there. You've never even paid a bill.
You'll lose the kids, the house, everything, and then who will take you in?
Everyone who tried that ended up on the street.
You won't last a month in that city.
what_it_is_not: Worry named as one's own: 'I'm anxious about the move, and I know it's your decision.'
An accurate warning about a real risk, such as a lease with penalties, with figures you can check.
A friend or relative asking hard questions about a plan, then helping you test it.
A financial adviser or lawyer laying out the realistic downsides of a risky choice.
A person with an anxiety condition who sees danger in most changes, including their own.
Advice you can verify that still leaves the choice with you.
this_may_be_it_when: The predicted outcome is far worse than the actual risk, and nobody explains how it would come about.
The warning appears when you take a step toward independence and rarely otherwise.
Your plans, savings and backup are brushed aside without being examined.
The prediction casts the speaker as the only safeguard.
You are told that no one else would help you or accept you.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They go through your plan with you, point out gaps, and then say the decision is yours.
Their worry is about specific, checkable risks.
They are just as anxious about their own changes.
They help you prepare for the risks they name.
A trusted third person independently sees the same risk.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Anxiety makes some people picture the worst, and they say it aloud to relieve themselves.
A parent who has seen things go wrong may want to protect an adult child without noticing the effect.
A person afraid of losing you may reach for the biggest warnings they can find.
People who had hard times themselves may assume yours will go the same way.
common_false_positives: A partner who says 'I'm scared about our finances if we both leave our jobs' and asks to make a plan.
A friend who warns you about an investment that looks like a scam, with details to check.
A relative who is nervous about you moving abroad but helps with the paperwork.
discernment_questions: Is this an account of a specific risk, or a general sense that I cannot cope?
Has anyone outside this relationship seen my plan and the risks?
Do these warnings come only when I move toward something of my own?
Have earlier predictions that came true been as bad as they were described?
What would I think if a friend were told the same thing about their plan?
less_concerning_if: Warnings include specifics you can check and a way to reduce the risk.
The speaker is as willing to hear that the plan might work as that it might fail.
Support continues after you decide, even if they would have chosen differently.
more_concerning_if: Predictions come with reduced access to money, papers, a phone, or contact with friends and family.
The warnings escalate to claims that you would lose children, home or safety if you left.
Earlier predictions did not come true, yet the same ones keep returning.
pattern_over_time_signs: You have stopped telling the person about your hopes and plans.
You have put off applying, studying, saving or moving.
You hear their predictions in your own voice when you think about change.
People close to you say you used to be more confident.
Catastrophizing as Control.repair_check: Pay attention to whether the forecasts turn into plans. A change sounds like 'I'm worried about money, can we look at the numbers together?', followed by the person supporting a choice that carries risk. A softer tone, with the prediction repeated whenever you move forward, leaves the fear installed.
Catastrophizing as Control.boundary_respect_check: Notice what happens when you ask to look at the actual risk together, with figures on paper. Is the conversation turned toward what could be done, or does the prediction grow? Also watch whether anything about your access to money, phone or friends changes afterwards.
Catastrophizing as Control.psychological_mechanism: Fear of loss is strong, and a confident forecast from someone close can sound like inside knowledge. Repeated, it can replace your own estimate of what you can handle, and uncertainty tends to get settled by staying put. When you are already unsure or financially dependent, the forecast fills the gap, and each step not taken makes the prediction feel truer.
Catastrophizing as Control.possible_impact_on_receiver: Feeling smaller, doubting your own competence, putting plans off and hearing a warning voice long after the conversation are all reported. Some felt unable to leave a job, a home or a relationship even when they wanted to. Others found out later that they managed far better than predicted, and felt anger and grief for the lost time.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the mechanics: 'What exactly do you think would go wrong, and what would help?' A specific worry can be checked, and a vague one tells you something too.
response_options.firm_boundary: Say how the predictions land: 'When you tell me I will fail, I feel less able to think. I'd like us to look at the facts instead.'
response_options.disengagement: You do not have to answer every prediction. A short 'I've heard you' lets the conversation move on, and you can work on your plans privately with someone you trust.
response_options.support_seeking: Show your plan, with the figures, to someone outside the relationship, such as a friend, a financial counselor or an advocate, and ask for an honest read of the risks. Keep a copy with a person the other party does not control.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, if a colleague or manager forecasts disaster whenever you apply for a role or take a project, ask for the specific risk in writing and seek an outside view from a mentor or HR.

Catastrophizing as Control.boundary_script: "I've heard that you're worried, and I want to understand the real risks. Can we write down what could go wrong and what would help with each one? I want to talk it over with my sister as well."
Catastrophizing as Control.safety_note: Predictions of ruin become a safety concern when they travel with control of money, papers, phones or transport, with monitoring, or with claims that you would lose children or housing if you left. Those can be signs of coercive control. A next step specific to this tactic: talk through your real options with a domestic abuse advocate or legal aid service, who can help you plan privately, before anything changes.
misuse_warning: A frank warning about a risky plan is not control. Labeling honest caution as a tactic can lead you to ignore real risks.
Do not use this label to dismiss an anxious relative who is trying, clumsily, to say that they care.
Catastrophizing as Control.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Emotional Blackmail attaches a penalty the speaker will impose, such as withdrawn love, if you do not comply; catastrophizing as control predicts a disaster that will arrive on its own. Guilt-Tripping looks back at blame for a harm already done, while this looks ahead to a ruin that has not happened. Pity Plays make the speaker the one who is suffering, where here you are the one forecast to fall. The difference is direction: a forecast about your future, offered as fact.
